newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Coffee nations mull extending quotas.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Coffee nations mull extending quotas.

text.p: Coffee nations held talks on Wednesday on proposals that they should extend a system of export quotas to try to lock in some of the gains from a spectacular rally in world prices.
The 14-nation Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) led by Brazil, the biggest seller, has to decide whether to extend current supply curbs beyond their expiry on June 30.

The London coffee talks are being held against a backdrop of a rally that has taken world prices for green (unroasted) beans up by 80-100 percent since January. Consumers are paying up to 50 percent more in the shops as roasters have passed on their higher costs.
Traders cite low stocks, tight supply of Latin American arabica beans and buying of coffee futures by speculative funds to explain the surprise bubble in the market.

Exporters are enjoying a windfall but worry that high prices could hit coffee demand. At the same time they have to consider what may happen to the market if the funds suddenly bale out, as they may later this year.
Ivory Coast Commodity Minister Guy-Alain Gauze said he would propose that quotas be kept.

Delegates said on Monday that an ACPC technical group had proposed that Wednesday's full meeting should adopt a draft plan that would retain quotas but try to make them more flexible, in view of the price volatility.

"I am going to propose to keep the quotas beyond June for the next six months," Gauze said as the talks resumed. He also favoured retaining an existing limit on total ACPC exports of 25.5 million bags.
Traders and analysts said that decisions now will be somewhat academic, with the market scrambling for every bean it can get and exporters disposed to ignore quotas and sell whatever they can.
But the market is likely to weaken later in the year, after the end of the upcoming frost season in Brazil.
At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee futures eased this week as fund investors already began to cash in profits. Coffee for July closed Tuesday at $2.40 a pound.
The now-expired May contract had hit $2.80 last week, the highest price on the exchange since June 1977.

"The market reached an extremely overbought region and basically it just corrected," said Walt Spilka, a Smith Barney analyst. "It comes down now to the weather in Brazil and, outside of a frost in Brazil, everything else is discounted."

Spilka said stocks of coffee had also been rising for the past week. Brokerage GNI Ltd said in a commentary that the real test of the ACPC would be not what it does now but "what it does when prices fall if the Brazilian crop survives frost damage this winter".
It had already achieved a measure of success because brokers were calling it a producer cartel, not an irrelevance, GNI said. - - London Newsroom+44 171 542 7729
